resources.string: Guide: How to Use Conditions and Build Queries

Welcome to the Visual Query Builder!

This panel helps you design SQL SELECT queries by choosing tables, columns, and filter conditions without writing SQL by hand.

  • Select main table: Chooses the primary table in the FROM clause.
  • Select columns: Check columns to display. If you select columns from another table, foreign keys will be traced to build JOIN clauses automatically.
  • Filters (WHERE): Add constraints using the \'Add Condition\' button.

Performs exact value comparisons.

  • How to use: Select a column, choose = (Equal) or != (Not Equal), and enter a target value.
  • Example: status = \'Active\' or role_id = 1.
  • Note: Text values will automatically be enclosed in single quotes.

Compares ranges of values, typically for numbers or date/time types.

  • Example: price > 500 or created_at >= \'2026-01-01\'.
  • Useful for finding high-value orders, recently registered users, etc.

Finds strings matching a specific pattern (case-sensitivity depends on DB engine).

  • How to use: Use % wildcard for any string of zero or more characters, or _ for a single character.
  • Examples:
    • Enter %An% to find names containing \'An\'.
    • Enter An% to find names starting with \'An\'.

Filters values within an inclusive range.

  • How to use: Enter two values separated by AND or a comma ,.
  • Examples:
    • Enter 10 AND 100 → translates to: col BETWEEN 10 AND 100
    • Enter 2026-01-01 AND 2026-05-31 → translates to: col BETWEEN \'2026-01-01\' AND \'2026-05-31\'

Checks if a column value matches any item in a list.

  • How to use: Enter values separated by commas ,.
  • Example: Enter Active, Pending → translates to: status IN (\'Active\', \'Pending\').
⭕ IS NULL / IS NOT NULL Operators

Checks if a field is empty (NULL) or populated.

  • Example: email IS NULL finds users without email addresses.
  • Note: Choosing this operator hides the value input field automatically.

Checks if a subquery returns any rows.

  • How to use: Select EXISTS or NOT EXISTS, and enter the full subquery text.
  • Subquery Example: SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE orders.user_id = users.id
  • Resulting SQL: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE orders.user_id = users.id)
  • Useful for checking related existence, such as users with orders vs users without orders.

Groups rows sharing identical values. Often used alongside aggregate functions like SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX.

  • How to use: Right-click columns in the order dialog to apply an aggregate (e.g. COUNT), then add the grouping column under \'GROUP BY\'.
  • Example: Counting customers by city:
    • Select columns: city and COUNT(id)
    • Add Group By row: choose city
    • Resulting SQL: SELECT city, COUNT(id) FROM users GROUP BY city

Sorts results in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order.

  • How to use: Click \'Add Sort\', pick a column, and choose direction.
  • You can sort by multiple columns (e.g., date descending, then name ascending).

Restricts the maximum number of rows returned.

  • Importance: In large datasets, loading all records can crash the app or exhaust memory. Adding a limit (e.g. 100) ensures snappy responses.
  • How to use: Enter a number in the \'Row Limit:\' box. Leave blank for no limit.
  • Automatically mapped to LIMIT N or TOP N syntax matching your DB dialet.
